questions.title: Valid Palindrome With One Deletion
questions.summary: Decide whether a string can become a palindrome after deleting at most one character.
questions.prompt: Given a string, return true when it is already a palindrome or can become one by deleting at most one character.

examples.explanation: Deleting b or c leaves a palindrome.

constraints: Treat the input as case-sensitive plain characters.

solutionTracks.title: Two Pointers With One Skip
solutionTracks.summary: Walk inward and spend the single allowed deletion only when the two boundary characters disagree.

steps.title: Compare boundaries
steps.explanation: Move left and right inward while characters match because the outside of the palindrome is already proven.

steps.title: Branch once on mismatch
steps.explanation: At the first mismatch, test the remaining substring after skipping the left character or the right character.

steps.title: Avoid extra branching
steps.explanation: After the skip is spent, the helper performs a plain palindrome check with no further deletions.

solutionTracks.explanation: Only the first mismatch can require the optional deletion. If skipping either side makes the middle a palindrome then one deletion is enough; otherwise no later decision can repair that boundary mismatch.

solutionTracks.title: Recursive Mismatch Budget
solutionTracks.summary: Model the deletion as a one-use budget and recurse only when the current pair of characters mismatches.

steps.title: Carry the budget
steps.explanation: The helper receives left, right, and whether the deletion has already been used.

steps.title: Recurse on mismatch
steps.explanation: When characters differ and the budget is unused, try consuming it on either side.

steps.title: Stop on exhausted budget
steps.explanation: A mismatch after the budget is spent means this path cannot form a palindrome.

solutionTracks.explanation: The recursive state describes exactly what remains to prove. Because the budget can branch only once, the solution still checks at most two linear substrings.

questions.title: Binary Tree Vertical Columns
questions.summary: Group binary tree nodes by their vertical column from left to right.
questions.prompt: Given a binary tree, return the node values grouped by vertical column from the leftmost column to the rightmost column.

examples.explanation: Nodes with the same horizontal offset share a column.

constraints: Preserve top-to-bottom order within a column for the BFS variant.

diagrams.title: Column coordinates
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[Root col 0] --> B[Left col -1]
  A --> C[Right col +1]
  C --> D[Left child col 0]

solutionTracks.title: BFS With Column Buckets
solutionTracks.summary: Traverse the tree by level while assigning each node a column index and collecting nodes by column.

steps.title: Attach coordinates
steps.explanation: Start the root at column zero; the left child is column minus one and the right child is column plus one.

steps.title: Preserve top-down order
steps.explanation: Use breadth-first traversal so nodes in the same column are appended in the order they are encountered by level.

steps.title: Emit sorted columns
steps.explanation: Track the smallest and largest column or sort the keys before building the final list.

solutionTracks.explanation: Column indexes group nodes that should appear together. BFS gives the expected top-to-bottom order inside each column without sorting every node by depth.

solutionTracks.title: DFS Then Sort Coordinates
solutionTracks.summary: Record each node as row, column, and value, then sort records into the requested vertical ordering.

steps.title: Record every coordinate
steps.explanation: Depth-first traversal writes a tuple containing column, row, and value for each node.

steps.title: Sort globally
steps.explanation: Sort by column first, then row, then value when a prompt requires tie-breaking among same-position nodes.

steps.title: Group by column
steps.explanation: Walk the sorted records and start a new output group whenever the column changes.

solutionTracks.explanation: The tuple contains every ordering dimension needed by the output. Once the records are sorted, grouping adjacent equal columns is deterministic.

python.label: Python
python.code:
def vertical_traversal(root):
    rows = []
    def dfs(node, row, col):
        if not node:
            return
        rows.append((col, row, node.val))
        dfs(node.left, row + 1, col - 1)
        dfs(node.right, row + 1, col + 1)
    dfs(root, 0, 0)
    ans = []
    last_col = None
    for col, row, value in sorted(rows):
        if col != last_col:
            ans.append([])
            last_col = col
        ans[-1].append(value)
    return ans

questions.title: Minimum Remove For Balanced Parentheses
questions.summary: Remove the fewest parentheses needed to make a mixed string valid.
questions.prompt: Given a string containing letters and parentheses, remove the minimum number of parentheses so the remaining string is balanced.

examples.explanation: The first closing parenthesis has no matching opening parenthesis.

constraints: Keep all non-parenthesis characters in their original order.

solutionTracks.title: Stack Of Unmatched Opens
solutionTracks.summary: Use a stack to remember unmatched opening characters and a set to mark characters that must be removed.

steps.title: Mark invalid closes
steps.explanation: When a closing character appears without an available opening character, mark that index for removal.

steps.title: Save unmatched opens
steps.explanation: Push opening indexes and pop one whenever a valid closing character matches it.

steps.title: Rebuild once
steps.explanation: After the scan, remove every marked index and every opening index left in the stack.

solutionTracks.explanation: A closing character is valid only if it can consume a previous unmatched opening character. Any leftover opening character also cannot be matched later, so rebuilding without those indexes creates a balanced string.

solutionTracks.title: Two Pass Filter
solutionTracks.summary: First remove invalid closing characters, then walk backward to remove extra opening characters.

steps.title: Filter left to right
steps.explanation: Append characters while maintaining a balance counter, skipping closing characters that would make balance negative.

steps.title: Filter right to left
steps.explanation: Walk the intermediate string backward and skip exactly the surplus opening characters.

steps.title: Reverse the result
steps.explanation: The backward pass builds the string in reverse order, so reverse it once before returning.

solutionTracks.explanation: The first pass guarantees no prefix has more closes than opens. The second pass removes the remaining surplus opens, so every prefix and the final balance are valid.
